advances: Proves the required two-cap inequality, including its complete equality family and all ray-boundary cases, for every triangle in the primary alternating parity \(P,N_x,N_y\). The proof uses no centroid-moment hypothesis. It is only a triangular lemma and asserts no localization or replacement of an arbitrary convex polygon by such a triangle.
author: mp_r76_two_cap_primary_triangle_fact
proof:
Put \(S=|T|\). The line \(x=0\) cuts off \(B\), the line \(y=0\) cuts off \(C\), and the line \(t=x+y=0\) cuts off \(A\). Therefore the respective cap areas are
\[
W_x+N_x+O,\qquad O+N_y+W_y,\qquad
P+W_x+W_y.
\]
The balance relation makes the first two equal. Define
\[
C_0=e+W_x+W_y+O,\qquad D=P+W_x+W_y.
\]
Then
\[
W_x+N_x+O=O+N_y+W_y=C_0
\]
and, after summing the six sectors,
\[
S=C_0+D+e.
\]
Normalize by
\[
c=\frac{C_0}{S},\qquad d=\frac{D}{S},\qquad
\varepsilon=\frac eS.
\]
Thus \(c,d,\varepsilon>0\) and
\[
c+d+\varepsilon=1.
\]
It suffices to prove
\[
c^2\ge4d\varepsilon. \tag{1}
\]

We first record the exact cap bound used below. Let \(z\) be an interior point of a triangle with positive barycentric coordinates \((a,r,s)\). Suppose a line through \(z\) cuts off the vertex having coordinate \(a\), and meets the two incident edges at fractions \(p,q\in(0,1]\) measured from that vertex. The normalized cap area is \(pq\), while the barycentric equation of the line gives
\[
\frac r p+\frac s q=1.
\]
Set \(X=r/p\). Then
\[
r\le X\le1-s,\qquad
pq=\frac{rs}{X(1-X)}.
\]
Maximizing \(X(1-X)\) on \([r,1-s]\) proves
\[
pq\ge m(r,s):=
\begin{cases}
4rs,&r\le1/2,\ s\le1/2,\\[2mm]
\dfrac{s}{1-r},&r>1/2,\\[2mm]
\dfrac{r}{1-s},&s>1/2.
\end{cases} \tag{2}
\]
The alternatives are exhaustive because \(r+s<1\). If \(r,s<1/2\), equality is unique and is characterized by
\[
\frac r p=\frac s q=\frac12,
\quad\text{equivalently}\quad p=2r,\ q=2s. \tag{3}
\]
If \(r\ge1/2\), equality in the corresponding limiting branch forces \(p=1\), so the cutting line passes through the endpoint having barycentric coordinate \(r\); the symmetric statement holds for \(s\ge1/2\). Formula (2) includes \(p=1\) and \(q=1\) exactly, not merely asymptotically.

Let \((\alpha,\beta,\gamma)\) be the barycentric coordinates of the origin relative to \(A,B,C\). Applying (2) to the three fan lines gives
\[
c\ge m(\alpha,\gamma),\qquad
c\ge m(\alpha,\beta),\qquad
d\ge m(\beta,\gamma). \tag{4}
\]

First, neither \(\beta\) nor \(\gamma\) can exceed \(1/2\). Indeed, if \(\beta>1/2\), then (4) gives
\[
c\ge\frac{\alpha}{\alpha+\gamma},
\qquad
d\ge\frac{\gamma}{\alpha+\gamma},
\]
contradicting \(c+d=1-\varepsilon<1\). The case \(\gamma>1/2\) is symmetric.

Suppose next that \(\alpha>1/2\). Then (4) gives
\[
c\ge
\max\left\{\frac{\beta}{\beta+\gamma},
\frac{\gamma}{\beta+\gamma}\right\}\ge\frac12.
\]
Consequently
\[
4d\varepsilon\le(d+\varepsilon)^2=(1-c)^2\le c^2,
\]
which proves (1) in this regime.

It remains to consider
\[
\alpha,\beta,\gamma\le\frac12.
\]
The argument is symmetric in \(\beta,\gamma\), so assume \(\beta\ge\gamma\). Put
\[
c_0=4\alpha\beta,\qquad d_0=4\beta\gamma.
\]
By (4),
\[
c\ge c_0,\qquad d\ge d_0. \tag{5}
\]
Moreover,
\[
2d_0+c_0=4\beta(\alpha+2\gamma)\ge1. \tag{6}
\]
To verify (6), substitute \(\gamma=1-\alpha-\beta\). The assumptions give
\[
\frac{1-\alpha}{2}\le\beta\le\frac12.
\]
The function
\[
4\beta(2-\alpha-2\beta)
\]
is concave in \(\beta\) and equals \(2(1-\alpha)\ge1\) at both endpoints of this interval. This proves (6), hence
\[
d_0\ge\frac{1-c_0}{2}.
\]

For
\[
F(c,d)=c^2-4d(1-c-d),
\]
one has
\[
\frac{\partial F}{\partial c}=2c+4d>0,
\qquad
\frac{\partial F}{\partial d}=8d-4(1-c)\ge0
\]
throughout the rectangle \(c\ge c_0,\ d\ge d_0\), where the last inequality follows from (6). Therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
F(c,d)
&\ge F(c_0,d_0)\\
&=16\beta(\beta-\gamma)
\bigl((1-\beta)^2-\beta\gamma\bigr)\ge0. \tag{7}
\end{aligned}
\]
The last inequality uses \(\beta\ge\gamma\) and
\[
(1-\beta)^2\ge\beta^2\ge\beta\gamma.
\]
Since \(\varepsilon=1-c-d\), inequality (7) is exactly (1).

We now determine equality. The regimes \(\beta>1/2\) and \(\gamma>1/2\) were impossible. If \(\alpha>1/2\), equality in the two inequalities
\[
4d\varepsilon\le(1-c)^2\le c^2
\]
would force \(c=1/2\), \(d=\varepsilon=1/4\), and \(\beta=\gamma\). Both side caps in (4) would then attain their minima. By the equality condition in (2), both \(x=0\) and \(y=0\) would pass through \(A\). Their only common point is the origin, contradicting that the origin is interior to \(T\).

In the remaining regime, the second factor in (7) is strictly positive: if \(\beta<1/2\), then
\[
(1-\beta)^2>\beta^2\ge\beta\gamma,
\]
while if \(\beta=1/2\), positivity of \(\alpha\) gives \(\gamma<1/2\) and again strictness. Equality in (7), in (5), and in the monotonicity of \(F\) therefore forces
\[
\beta=\gamma=\frac{1-\alpha}{2},\qquad
c=4\alpha\beta,\qquad d=4\beta\gamma. \tag{8}
\]
If \(\alpha=1/2\), equality in the two side-cap bounds again makes both \(x=0\) and \(y=0\) pass through \(A\), which is impossible. Hence, writing
\[
u=\alpha,\qquad r=1-u,\qquad a=1-2u,
\]
one has \(0<u<1/2\), \(\beta=\gamma=r/2\), and all three cap minima are the unique minima described in (3).

Let \((\lambda_A,\lambda_B,\lambda_C)\) be barycentric coordinates on \(T\). Equality for the \(t=0\) cap says that this line has equation
\[
\frac{\lambda_B}{r}+\frac{\lambda_C}{r}=1,
\quad\text{or equivalently}\quad \lambda_A=u.
\]
Since \(t(A)>0\), there is a number \(\rho>0\) such that
\[
t=\rho(\lambda_A-u). \tag{9}
\]
Equality for the \(x=0\) and \(y=0\) caps says that their equations are respectively
\[
L_x:=\frac{\lambda_A}{2u}+\frac{\lambda_C}{r}-1=0,
\qquad
L_y:=\frac{\lambda_A}{2u}+\frac{\lambda_B}{r}-1=0.
\]
Thus \(x=\xi L_x\) and \(y=\eta L_y\) for some \(\xi,\eta>0\). Evaluating \(t=x+y\) at \(B\) and \(C\), whose \(t\)-coordinates both equal \(-\rho u\) by (9), gives \(\xi=\eta\). Evaluation at \(A\) then gives
\[
\xi=\eta=\frac{\rho r u}{a}.
\]
It follows that \(q=x-y\) takes the values
\[
q(A)=0,\qquad q(B)=-\frac{\rho u}{a},\qquad
q(C)=\frac{\rho u}{a}.
\]
Together with (9), these are exactly the three vertices stated in the equality classification.

Conversely, fix \(\rho>0\) and \(0<u<1/2\), and let \(T\) have those vertices. It is enough to calculate at \(\rho=1\), since all areas scale by \(\rho^2\). With \(r=1-u\), \(a=1-2u\), and
\[
h(t)=\frac{u}{a}(r-t),
\]
the triangle is
\[
-u\le t\le r,\qquad |q|\le h(t),
\]
and the physical area element is \(\frac12\,dt\,dq\). The fan lines are \(t=0\) and \(q=\pm t\). Since \(h(t)\ge t\) exactly for \(0\le t\le u\), and \(h(t)\ge -t\) for \(-u\le t\le0\), direct integration gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
P
&=\int_0^u t\,dt+\int_u^r h(t)\,dt
=\frac{ru}{2},\\
W_x=W_y
&=\frac12\int_0^u\bigl(h(t)-t\bigr)\,dt
=\frac{ru^2}{4a},\\
O
&=\int_{-u}^0(-t)\,dt
=\frac{u^2}{2},\\
N_x=N_y
&=\frac12\int_{-u}^0\bigl(h(t)+t\bigr)\,dt
=\frac{u^2(1+u)}{4a}.
\end{aligned} \tag{10}
\]
Restoring the factor \(\rho^2\), formulas (10) yield
\[
e=\frac{\rho^2u^3}{2a},\qquad
C_0=\frac{\rho^2ru^2}{a},\qquad
D=\frac{\rho^2r^2u}{2a}.
\]
Thus \(e>0\), the balance relation holds, and \(C_0^2=4eD\). This proves both directions of the equality classification.

It remains to justify the ray-boundary cases. For a nonzero point of \(\overline{N_x}\) one has \(x<0\), for a nonzero point of \(\overline{N_y}\) one has \(y<0\), and for a nonzero point of \(\overline P\) one has \(t>0\). The other two vertices lie in the corresponding closed opposite halfplane. They cannot both lie on the cutting fan line, because their joining edge would then contain the origin, contrary to the origin being interior to \(T\). Hence each fan line still cuts the stated vertex and has intersection fractions \(p,q\in(0,1]\). A boundary vertex gives exactly \(p=1\) or \(q=1\), already covered by (2). Thus every boundary-ray case is included without a balance-breaking perturbation; equivalently, its cap formula is the exact endpoint limit as the relevant fraction tends to \(1\). The equality analysis shows that no such endpoint case attains equality.

Finally, the centroid of an equality triangle has
\[
t(G)=\frac{\rho(1-3u)}3,\qquad q(G)=0,
\]
and hence
\[
x(G)=y(G)=\frac{\rho(1-3u)}6.
\]
Because \(\int_Tx\,dA=Sx(G)\) and \(\int_Ty\,dA=Sy(G)\), either nonnegative centroid-moment hypothesis is equivalent on this family to \(u\le1/3\). Neither hypothesis appeared anywhere in the proof of (1).
statement:
Use the six rays and sector names of accepted fact `f93a19566af88e9a`:
\[
r_0=(1,0),\quad r_1=(0,1),\quad r_2=(-1,1),\quad
r_3=(-1,0),\quad r_4=(0,-1),\quad r_5=(1,-1),
\]
with sectors \(P,W_x,N_x,O,N_y,W_y\) in cyclic order. Let
\[
T=\operatorname{conv}\{A,B,C\}
\]
be a nondegenerate triangle containing the origin in its interior, where
\[
A\in\overline P,\qquad B\in\overline{N_x},\qquad
C\in\overline{N_y}.
\]
Write the same six capital letters for the corresponding sector areas of \(T\), and suppose
\[
N_x-W_y=N_y-W_x=:e>0.
\]
Then
\[
(e+W_x+W_y+O)^2\ge 4e(P+W_x+W_y).
\]

Equality holds if and only if there are \(\rho>0\) and \(u\in(0,1/2)\) such that, in the coordinates
\[
t=x+y,\qquad q=x-y,
\]
the vertices \(A,B,C\) have respective coordinates
\[
\bigl(\rho(1-u),0\bigr),\qquad
\left(-\rho u,-\frac{\rho u}{1-2u}\right),\qquad
\left(-\rho u,\frac{\rho u}{1-2u}\right).
\]
In particular, every equality triangle has its three vertices in the open sectors \(P,N_x,N_y\); hence the inequality is strict if any vertex is on a boundary ray.

Neither of the original centroid-moment assumptions
\[
\int_T x\,dA\ge0,\qquad \int_T y\,dA\ge0
\]
is needed for the inequality. On the equality family above, either one of these two assumptions is equivalent to \(u\le1/3\). Thus imposing both assumptions restricts the equality family precisely to \(0<u\le1/3\), and does nothing else in this triangular proof.
